blocks.text: Bipyramids

DOI: 10.1002/smll.200700379
Growth of Gold Bipyramids with Improved Yield and
Their Curvature-Directed Oxidation

Xiaoshan Kou, Weihai Ni, Chia-Kuang Tsung, Kong Chan, Hai-Qing Lin,
Galen D. Stucky, and Jianfang Wang*

The surface-plasmon properties of Au bipyramids are investigated using
the finite-difference time-domain method. It is found that both the extinc-
tion cross sections and local electric-field enhancements of Au bipyramids
are larger than those of Au nanorods that have longitudinal surface
plasmon (LSP) wavelengths close to those of Au bipyramids. Following
this result the growth of Au bipyramids using cationic surfactants of
variously sized headgroups as stabilizing agents is carried out. It is found
that the growth using cetyltributylammonium bromide (CTBAB)
produces Au bipyramids with tunable LSP wavelengths in high yields.
The oxidation behaviour of Au bipyramids using hydrogen peroxide as
the oxidizing agent is fully explored and the oxidation is found to occur
preferentially at highly curved surface sites. It is further demonstrated that
the oxidation rate can be controlled by varying the amounts of hydrogen
peroxide and hydrochloric acid. This oxidation approach can be used in
conjunction with the seed-mediated growth in CTBAB solutions to
produce Au bipyramids, the LSP wavelengths of which are finely tunable
from 650 to 1300 nm.

Keywords:
· bipyramids
· gold
· oxidation
· surface plasmon resonance
· surfactants
1. Introduction

Gold nanorods exhibit strong optical extinction at their
longitudinal surface plasmon (LSP) wavelengths, which are
tunable from the visible to near-infrared region by varying
their aspect ratios. They have been demonstrated to func-

tion as scattering[1,2] and two-photon-absorption[3] chromo-
phores for biological imaging of blood vessels and cancer
cells, biological sensors,[4,5] carriers for drug delivery,[6] and
agents for photothermal cancer therapy.[2] They have been
incorporated into polymers to create hybrid optical materi-
als[7] and deposited onto bacteria to create bioelectronic ma-
terials.[8] They have been assembled onto flat surfaces to
function as substrates for surface-enhanced Raman spectros-
copy (SERS).[9] In addition, interesting chain[5,10,11] and ring
structures[12] have been formed from Au nanorods using
templates or various thiol molecules.
The electric field in the region close to the surfaces of
noble metal nanostructures is enhanced relative to the far
field when they are illuminated at their surface-plasmon
wavelengths. For Au nanorods, such local field enhance-
ments, as well as their extinction cross sections and surface-
plasmon wavelengths, are essential for realizing their poten-

tial optical and biotechnological applications. In general,
large field enhancements are beneficial to SERS and two-
photon luminescence imaging, and high extinction cross sec-
tions are favourable for scattering-based imaging. Therefore,
Au nanostructures that exhibit both larger local field en-
hancements and extinction cross sections than Au nanorods
and also possess tunable surface-plasmon wavelengths simi-
lar to Au nanorods are highly desired.
Gold bipyramids have a pentagonal base and two sharp
apexes. Similar to Au nanorods, bipyramids also possess two
surface-plasmon resonances corresponding to the electron
oscillations along the longitudinal and transverse directions.
The LSP wavelengths can be tuned systematically by vary-
ing the ratio of the height to the base-edge length. Because
the apexes of Au bipyramids are sharper than the ends of
nanorods, the local electric-field enhancements associated
with bipyramids should be larger than that associated with
nanorods, according to the lightning-rod effect.[13] Au bipyr-
amids should thus be more advantageous than Au nanorods
for two-photon luminescence imaging and SERS.
A seed-mediated method has previously been used to
grow Au bipyramids in aqueous solutions using cationic sur-
factants as stabilizing agents in the presence of AgNO3.[14,15]

The growth using citrate-stabilized Au nanoparticle seeds in
cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) solutions produ-
ces Au bipyramids with LSP wavelengths in the range of
750–850 nm and yields of 30%. Cetyltriethylammonium
bromide (CTEAB) has also been used as a stabilizing agent
to grow Au bipyramids.[16] The LSP wavelengths of the re-
sulting bipyramids can be varied from 700 to 1100 nm by
changing the amount of seeds relative to that of the Au pre-
cursor. However, the maximum yields of bipyramids are
below 30%, and the yields decrease rapidly for bipyramids
with longer LSP wavelengths.
We have previously used cetyltripropylammonium bro-
mide
(CTPAB)
and
cetyltributylammonium
bromide
(CTBAB) surfactants to grow Au nanorods using CTAB-
stabilized Au nanoparticle seeds through the seed-mediated
method.[17] These surfactants have larger headgroups than
CTAB and CTEAB. A systematic comparison of the nano-
rod growth using these four surfactants indicates that the
average aspect ratios of the Au nanorods increase and the
nanorod growth rates decrease as the surfactant headgroup
gets larger. The reason for this headgroup size-dependent
nanorod-growth behaviour has been postulated to be that
the bilayers formed on the surfaces of Au nanorods from
the surfactants with larger headgroups are more stable. On
the basis of these previous observations, we expect that the
seed-mediated growth using CTPAB and CTBAB as stabi-
lizing agents might produce Au bipyramids with LSP wave-
lengths tunable over a broader spectral range and in im-
proved yields.
In this paper, we first present the results of finite-differ-
ence time-domain (FDTD) calculations performed on Au
bipyramids and nanorods that have similar LSP wave-
lengths. We then describe the growth of Au bipyramids in
CTBAB solutions using citrate-stabilized Au nanoparticle
seeds through the seed-mediated method. Finally, curvature-
directed oxidation of Au bipyramids using hydrogen perox-

ide as the oxidizing agent is demonstrated. The oxidation
rate is shown to be dependent on the amount of the oxidiz-
ing agent, the acid concentration, the stabilizing surfactant,
and the type of Au nanostructures. This oxidation approach
allows us to produce Au bipyramids with their LSP wave-
lengths finely controlled between 650 and 1300 nm.
2. Results and Discussion
2.1. FDTD Calculation

The surface-plasmon properties of Au bipyramids and
nanorods were investigated and compared using the FDTD
method. The FDTD method can be used to calculate the
optical response of noble metal nanostructures of arbitrary
geometries to an incident light wave.[18] Surface-plasmon
properties such as absorption and scattering cross sections
as well as local electric-field enhancements can be obtained
from this method. Such properties are generally difficult to
measure experimentally but they are very important for the
creation of optical and biotechnological materials and de-

Gold bipyramids and nanorods of representative sizes
that are readily available from the seed-mediated growth
were chosen for FDTD calculation. Their transmission elec-

and shape distributions of the bipyramids are narrower than

For FDTD calculation, the sizes of the bipyramid and
nanorod were taken to be as close as possible to their re-
spective average values obtained from TEM imaging. Spe-
cifically, the height and base edge length of the bipyramid
are 87 and 20.4 nm, respectively, and its apex angle is 308.
Its apexes were modelled as spherical caps with five cut
facets. The diameter of the capped sphere is 14.1 nm, which
is determined by the height and apex angle of the bipyra-
mid. The length and diameter of the nanorod are 42 and
12 nm, respectively. Its ends are modelled as half spheres.
Figure 1C and D show the extinction curves obtained from
the FDTD calculation at a mesh size of 0.5 nm for the bipyr-
amid and nanorod, respectively (see also Supporting Infor-
mation (SI), Figure S1 and S2). The extinction spectrum of
the bipyramid in the region of the longitudinal surface-plas-
mon resonance is similar to that of the nanorod. The calcu-
lated LSP peak wavelengths at 773 and 775 nm (Table 1)
are both blue-shifted relative to the ensemble values for the
bipyramid and nanorod, respectively. This is because, in
general, larger bipyramids and nanorods have larger extinc-
tion cross sections. They contribute more to the extinction
spectrum than smaller ones during ensemble measurements.
On the other hand, the average sizes of the bipyramid and
nanorod used for the FDTD calculation are determined
from TEM imaging, where particles of different sizes are
sampled at an equal probability. This causes a blue-shift in
the FDTD-calculated LSP relative to that obtained from en-
semble measurements for both the bipyramid and nanorod.
Moreover, the FWHMs obtained from the FDTD calcula-
tion are 47 nm (97 meV) and 45 nm (93 meV) for the bipyr-
amid and nanorod, respectively (Table 1). For comparison,
the homogeneous FWHMs obtained previously by measur-
ing the white-light scattering spectra from individual bipyra-
mids[15] and nanorods[19] of similar LSP wavelengths are 100
and 80 meV, respectively. The FWHMs measured from the

ensemble
samples
are
larger
than
the
homogeneous
FWHMs obtained from individual bipyramids and nanorods,
suggesting that the ensemble bipyramid and nanorod sam-
ples have an inhomogeneous size and shape distribution.
A marked difference between the bipyramid and nano-
rod is that the extinction cross section of the bipyramid is
about 6 times that of the nanorod at their LSP wavelengths
(Table 1). Au nanorods have previously been treated ap-
proximately as ellipsoids and Gans@ theory has been used to
analyze their surface plasmon properties.[20] According to
Gans@ theory, the extinction cross section of an ellipsoid is
proportional to its volume. The volume of the bipyramid
used for FDTD calculation is about 6 times that of the
nanorod. Therefore, the difference in the extinction cross
section between the bipyramid and nanorod obtained from
FDTD calculation is in agreement with that predicated by
Gans@ theory.
The local electric-field-intensity enhancement contours
associated with the LSP resonance are shown in Figure 2
and SI Figure S3 for the averagely sized Au bipyramid and
nanorod. The propagation direction of the incident light
wave is perpendicular to the longitudinal direction and its
polarization is parallel to the longitudinal direction. It is
seen that the bipyramid supports a very strong local field
enhancement at its apexes, with a maximal intensity en-
hancement value of 6100. In comparison, the maximal field
intensity enhancement of the nanorod at its ends is 1700
(Table 1). The field intensity enhancement supported by the
bipyramid is 3.6 times that by the nanorod. The field en-
hancement exhibited by the bipyramid is comparable to that
reported recently for hematite-Au core/shell prolate spher-
oidal nanostructures[21] and is several times larger than
those reported previously for bowtie junctions fabricated
using electron beam lithography.[22] Such strong local field
enhancements make Au bipyramids highly attractive for use
in designing substrates for SERS and creating hybrid mate-
rials with enhanced nonlinear optical properties.
We further performed FDTD calculations on a nanorod
whose volume is approximately equal to that of the average-
ly sized Au bipyramid in order to investigate if the particle
volume has an effect on the local electric-field enhance-
ment. The length and diameter of the Au nanorod were
chosen to be 78 and 22 nm, respectively, so that its volume
and LSP peak wavelength are close to those of the bipyra-
mid (Figure 1E, SI Figure S4, and Table 1). It is seen that
the maximal field intensity enhancement of this larger nano-
rod is about one sixth that of the bipyramid, indicating that
the maximal field enhancement is mainly determined by the

2.2. Growth of Gold Bipyramids

It is seen from FDTD calculations that Au bipyramids
exhibit larger electric-field enhancements and extinction

cross sections than nanorods at similar LSP wavelengths. Au
bipyramids are therefore more favourable for optical appli-
cations where large extinction cross sections and high elec-
tric-field enhancements are desired. Au bipyramids have
previously been grown in CTAB and CTEAB solutions
using a seed-mediated method.[14–16] However, the yields of
bipyramids with LSP wavelengths in the range of 750–
850 nm are limited below 30%, and the yields decrease
rapidly for bipyramids with longer LSP wavelengths.
Hydrochloric acid has been used during the growth of
Au bipyramids in CTAB solutions with ascorbic acid as a re-
ducing agent.[15] The presence of hydrochloric acid can slow
down the growth and increase the yield of Au bipyramids
due to the decrease in the reducing capability of ascorbic
acid. On the other hand, it has been found that the use of
cationic surfactants with increasingly larger headgroups can
slow down the growth of Au nanorods.[17] The binding of
surfactants to the surfaces of Au nanorods gets stronger as
the headgroups become larger, probably due to reduced
electrostatic repulsion among the headgroups. We therefore
carried out the growth of Au bipyramids using CTBAB as a
stabilizing agent. Figure 3 shows the extinction spectra of

the Au bipyramids grown in CTBAB solutions with varying
volumes of the citrate-stabilized seed solution. As the
volume of the seed solution is reduced, the LSP peak of the
Au bipyramids shifts to the longer wavelength. A tunable
range of 800–1300 in the LSP wavelength can be readily
achieved during our growth. More remarkably, as the LSP
peak wavelength becomes longer, the extinction values at
both the longer-wavelength and shorter-wavelength peaks
remain almost constant around 2.8 and 1.6, respectively.
This suggests that the yields of the Au bipyramids remain
approximately constant as they grow larger because the
longer-wavelength extinction peak is solely due to the LSP
resonance of the bipyramids and the shorter-wavelength
peak is contributed by both the transverse plasmon reso-
nance of the bipyramids and the plasmon resonance of the
roughly spherical Au nanoparticles that were grown togeth-
er with the bipyramids. In addition, the FWHMs of the LSP
peaks of the bipyramids are in the range of 80–180 nm,

Ascorbic acid was used as the reducing agent for the
seed-mediated growth of Au bipyramids. The stoichiometric
molar ratio of ascorbic acid to HAuCl4 is 1.5 according to
the redox reaction.[26] However, it has been found in our ex-
periments that a molar ratio of ascorbic acid to HAuCl4
above 3.0 is generally beneficial to the growth of Au bipyra-
mids with tunable LSP wavelengths in high yields. If the
molar ratio of ascorbic acid to HAuCl4 is reduced to be
close to the stoichiometric value, the yields of bipyramids
with longer LSP wavelengths decrease considerably (SI Fig-
ure S5).
We further carried out the seed-mediated growth experi-
ments using CTAB, CTEAB, and CTPAB surfactants as sta-
bilizing agents (SI Figure S6–8). By taking together the
growth results in the solutions of the four surfactants, it is
seen that the yields of Au bipyramids generally increase as
the surfactant headgroup becomes larger. CTBAB has the
largest headgroup, and the yield of Au bipyramids grown in
CTBAB solutions is the highest among the four surfactants.
This is exactly what we have expected. During growth, sur-
factants form a bilayer on the surfaces of bipyramids.[27] The
positively charged headgroups in the inner layer are bound
to the surfaces through electrostatic interactions. The in-
crease in the yields of Au bipyramids probably results from
the stronger binding of the surfactants to the surfaces of bi-
pyramids as their headgroups get larger.[17]
2.3. Oxidation of Gold Bipyramids

The ability to tailor the shapes and sizes of inorganic
nanostructures is critical to modern materials chemistry be-
cause the intrinsic properties of most nanostructures are
strongly dependent on their shapes and sizes. A very popu-
lar approach that has been used is the formation of nuclei
from atoms and molecules at the first stage, followed by
growth into variously shaped nanostructures at the second
stage through careful control of the growth rates along dif-
ferent lattice directions. In addition to this general growth
approach, reshaping and resizing through chemical reactions
can also be used to make inorganic nanostructures of vari-
ous shapes and sizes. For example, it has been demonstrated
that Au nanorods can be shortened to produce nanorods of
smaller aspect ratios through anisotropic oxidation reac-
tions.[24,28] One advantage of the shortening approach to the
preparation of Au nanorods is that the shortening process
can be monitored in real time and nanorods of any aspect
ratio smaller than that of starting nanorods can be obtained.
We carried out the oxidation experiments on the Au bi-
pyramids grown in CTBAB solutions in order to obtain bi-
pyramids of finely tuned LSP wavelengths and compare the

oxidation behaviour of bipyramids with that of nanorods.
Cyanide, persulfate, AuIII, and oxygen have been used in
previous experiments to oxidize Au nanorods.[24,28] H2O2 was
chosen in our experiments to oxidize Au bipyramids be-
cause it is nontoxic and easy to handle. Figure 5A and B

show the extinction spectra taken as a function of time for
the oxidation using two different amounts of H2O2. The
LSP and transverse plasmon peak wavelengths of the start-
ing Au bipyramids are around 1000 and 590 nm, respective-
ly. During oxidation, the LSP peak exhibits a significant
blue-shift, while the transverse plasmon peak only blue-
shifts slightly. Both peaks decrease in intensity. With con-
tinuing oxidation, the LSP peak becomes a shoulder of the
transverse plasmon peak and finally disappears, suggesting
the transformation of bipyramids into nanospheres. Au
nanospheres are eventually completely oxidized, as indicat-
ed by the disappearance of the single extinction peak
around 530 nm. Moreover, a weak peak appears around
400 nm with oxidation, and it becomes stronger and stronger
throughout the oxidation process. This peak results from the
metal–ligand charge-transfer absorption of HAuBr4, indicat-
ing the oxidation of Au0 to AuIII.
The extinction spectra shown in Figure 5A and B were
taken every 30 min. It is seen that the blue-shift in the LSP
wavelength is faster as the amount of H2O2 used for oxida-
tion is increased. To quantify the oxidation rate, we plotted

The oxidation rate of Au bipyramids can not only be
changed by varying the amount of H2O2, but also by adding
HCl. Figure 6A and B show the evolutionary extinction
spectra acquired for the oxidation with the addition of HCl.
The pH of as-grown Au bipyramid solutions is 3–4. The oxi-
dation rate is increased several times if the solution pH is
adjusted to 2 by the addition of a small amount of HCl
(Table 2). The faster oxidation of Au bipyramids obtained
by the addition of HCl is because the oxidizing capability of
H2O2 is enhanced by the increase in the acid concentration.
Our demonstrated ability to control the oxidation rate is
very useful for the production of Au bipyramids with finely
tuned LSP wavelengths. It has been shown above that the
LSP wavelengths of Au bipyramids can also be tailored
during growth by varying the amount of seeds relative to
that of the Au precursor. However, we have found that the
LSP wavelengths of Au bipyramids that are grown following
the same procedure often vary from batch to batch due to
unavoidable fluctuations in growth conditions. In addition,
the tuning of the LSP wavelength by varying the amount of
seed is discrete in nature, while that through oxidation is
continuous. A combination of these two approaches makes
possible the preparation of Au bipyramids with LSP wave-
lengths controlled precisely over a wide spectral range from
650 to 1300 nm.
Au bipyramids at varying stages of oxidation can be ob-
tained by centrifugation and redispersion into aqueous solu-
tions if the oxidation rate is sufficiently small. The resulting
samples exhibit vivid colors (SI Figure S10). The evolution
of their morphologies and sizes was monitored using TEM
(Figure 7A–F). Oxidation at the early stage mainly occurs

at the apexes of bipyramids. The apexes become blunter
and the bipyramids are shortened (Figure 7A). With con-
tinuing oxidation, the apexes of the bipyramids are further
blunted. The vertexes at the base and the side edges are
gradually smoothed (Figure 7B and C). As a result, the bi-
pyramids become ellipsoidal. After this stage, the ellipsoids
shrink in both their major and minor axes (Figure 7D and
E). Finally they become spheres (Figure 7F). It is clear
from TEM imaging that the oxidation reaction preferential-
ly occurs at surface sites with high curvature, so that sharp
apexes and edges gradually disappear and smoother surfaces
are produced. Such curvature-directed oxidation has also
been observed previously during the oxidation of Au nano-
rods using AuIII and oxygen, where the length of nanorods is
reduced gradually while the diameter remains almost un-

3. Conclusions

The LSP properties of Au bipyramids and nanorods with
similar LSP wavelengths have been investigated using the
FDTD method. When excited at their LSP wavelengths, Au
bipyramids exhibit a maximal electric-field-intensity en-

hancement that is 3–6 times that of Au nanorods. The field-
intensity enhancement associated with the LSP resonance is
mainly determined by the particle shape instead of the par-
ticle volume. Encouraged by this result, we have used
CTBAB as a stabilizing agent to prepare Au bipyramids
with a seed-mediated growth method. The yields of the re-
sulting bipyramids are 50–60% and they remain nearly un-
changed when the LSP wavelengths of the bipyramids are
tailored from 800 to 1300 nm by varying the seed amount.
Oxidation experiments have further been carried out on
CTBAB-stabilized Au bipyramids using H2O2 as the oxidiz-
ing agent. It has been found that oxidation preferentially
occurs at surface sites with high curvature. The oxidation
rate of Au bipyramids can be controlled by varying the
amount of H2O2 and HCl. It has also been found that with
the same amount of H2O2, the oxidation rate increases in
the order of CTBAB-stabilized Au bipyramids, CTBAB-sta-
bilized Au nanorods, and CTAB-stabilized Au nanorods.
This oxidation approach can be used together with the seed-
mediated growth in CTBAB solutions to produce Au bipyr-
amids with LSP wavelengths finely controlled from 650 to
1300 nm.

4. Experimental Section

FDTD calculation: A software package, FDTD Solutions, devel-
oped by Lumerical Solutions, Inc., was employed to carry out
FDTD calculations on Au bipyramids and nanorods. The gold di-
electric function was represented using a Drude model,[18] with
parameters chosen to match bulk dielectric data measured previ-
ously.[29] The refractive index of the surrounding medium, water,
was taken to be 1.33. An electromagnetic pulse was launched in
a box around a target Au nanostructure to simulate a propagat-
ing plane wave interacting with the nanostructure. Only the LSP
resonance was calculated by setting the electric field of the
plane wave parallel to the longitudinal direction. The nanorod
was modeled as a cylinder capped with a half sphere at each
end. The apexes of the bipyramid were modeled as spherical
caps with five cut facets. Their sizes were taken to match the
average values measured from TEM images as closely as possi-
ble. Different mesh sizes were used for each nanostructure. The
changes of various parameters, including the plasmon wave-
length, extinction cross section, line width, and field-intensity
enhancement, as a function of the mesh size were obtained. For
small mesh sizes, graded meshes were employed, where the
size of the mesh cells on the target nanostructure was smaller
than that in the surrounding region. Such nonuniform meshes
can make FDTD calculation more accurate, while requiring less
memory and less computation time than comparable uniform
meshes.
Growth of gold bipyramids: Gold bipyramids were grown
using the seed-mediated method in aqueous cationic surfactant
solutions in the presence of AgNO3. CTEAB, CTPAB, and CTBAB
were synthesized by refluxing stoichiometric amounts of 1-bro-
mohexadecane and corresponding trialkylamine in dry acetoni-
trile, as reported previously.[17] Citrate-stabilized Au nanoparti-
cles were used as seeds. Their preparation followed the previ-
ously reported procedure.[15,16] Briefly, aqueous solutions of
HAuCl4 (0.01m, 0.125 mL) and sodium citrate (0.01m, 0.25 mL)
were first added into deionized water (9.625 mL), and then a
freshly prepared, ice-cold solution of NaBH4 (0.01m, 0.15 mL)
was added under vigorous stirring. The resulting seed solution
was kept for at least 2 h before use. For a typical preparation of
Au bipyramids in CTBAB solutions, a growth solution was first
prepared by the addition of aqueous solutions of HAuCl4
(0.01m, 0.3 mL), ascorbic acid (0.1m, 0.1 mL), and AgNO3
(0.01m, 0.45 mL) into an aqueous CTBAB solution (0.01m,
7.125 mL). The citrate-stabilized seed solution (0.075 mL) was
then added. The reaction solution was mixed by gentle inversion
for 10 s and then left undisturbed overnight in an isothermal
oven at 658C. Similar preparations with the use of different vol-
umes of the ascorbic acid and seed solutions were carried out in
order to investigate the effects of the amounts of ascorbic acid
and the seeds on the growth of Au bipyramids in CTBAB solu-
tions. This preparation procedure was also followed to grow Au
bipyramids in CTAB, CTEAB, and CTPAB solutions, respectively,
where the concentrations of the three surfactants were 0.1m and
the growth was at room temperature.
Growth of gold nanorods: CTAB-stabilized Au nanorods were
grown as reported previously,[24,30] and CTBAB-stabilized Au

nanorods were prepared according to our previously reported
procedure.[17]

Oxidation of gold bipyramids and nanorods: As-grown Au bi-
pyramid
and
nanorod
solutions
were
used
for
oxidation.
35 wt.% H2O2 was used as the oxidizing agent. Oxidation was
carried out by the addition of the H2O2 solution into Au bipyra-
mid and nanorod solutions. The oxidation process was moni-
tored by taking extinction spectra as a function time. The volume
of the H2O2 solution was varied and different volumes of HCl
(1m) was added in order to control the oxidation rate.
Characterization: Extinction spectra were taken on a Hitachi
U-3501 UV/Vis/NIR spectrophotometer. Rectangular quartz cuv-
ettes with an optical path length of 1 cm were used. Low-mag-
nification TEM images were acquired using a FEI CM120 micro-
scope at 120 kV, and they were used to determine the yields
and sizes of Au nanostructures. HRTEM images were recorded
using a TECNAI 20 ST microscope at 200 kV. For TEM characteri-
zation, as-grown and oxidized Au bipyramid solutions (6 mL
each) were centrifuged at 12000 g for 6 min. The precipitates
were redispersed in deionized water (6 mL each), centrifuged
again at 12000 D g for 6 min, and finally redispersed in deion-
ized water (0.4 mL each). 0.01 mL of each resulting bipyramid
solution was drop-cast onto a lacey-formvar carbon-stabilized
TEM grid and allowed to dry in air overnight.
